title: Liquid Glass vs Glassmorphism
lede: These two names get used interchangeably, and on a screenshot they nearly are. The difference appears when you look at where each one puts its depth: one builds it into the border, the other hangs it outside the card.
verdict: Glassmorphism floats — a large soft outer shadow, a hover lift, and a light streak that fades at both ends. Liquid Glass sits — a hard uniform top highlight, a heavier border, and no shadow at all.
brief: Both styles are the same three ingredients: a saturated field behind the page, translucent panels above it, and backdrop-filter to blur what is behind. That is why they read as siblings and why most comparisons end in a shrug.

The divergence is in the edge. In this gallery the Glassmorphism card draws its top light with a ::before element using a horizontal gradient that fades out at both ends, and then lifts the card 4px on hover above a 50px soft shadow. The Liquid Glass card does neither: it paints a single uniform line with box-shadow: inset 0 1px 0 at 55 percent, keeps the card still, and relies on a 28 percent border to separate it from the field.

dimensions.name: Top edge light
dimensions.a: One uniform 1px inset line at 55% white, full width
dimensions.b: A gradient streak that fades to transparent at both ends

dimensions.name: Depth cue
dimensions.a: Inside the border — the panel reads as thick material
dimensions.b: Outside the card — a 50px soft shadow, so it floats

cssDelta.label: Top light
cssDelta.b: ::before { height:1px; background: linear-gradient(90deg, transparent, rgba(255,255,255,.75), transparent) }

whenA: The panel is large and sits over a photographic or video background, where a soft shadow would smear into the image
You want the card to read as a physical slab — a panel of frosted acrylic rather than a floating sheet
The page has many stacked panels; hover lifts on every one become a nervous, fidgety surface
whenB: The card is small and needs to separate from a busy field — the soft shadow does that work at a glance
You want a hover affordance on a grid of cards, where the lift reads as clickable
The background is dark and flat, so a 50px shadow has somewhere to fall and does not look like dirt
promptDelta: The words that steer a model between these are specific: ask for a single inset top highlight with no drop shadow and no hover transform, and you get Liquid Glass. Ask for a gradient streak on the top edge plus a large soft shadow and a 4px hover lift, and you get Glassmorphism. Naming the material rather than the style — slab versus pane — gets you there faster than naming the style at all, because both names are ambiguous enough that a model will pick either.
